综合写作 4

In recent decades, engineers in Canada have begun extracting oil from deposits called tar sands. These are sandy deposits that contain a very thick, almost solid form of oil. Extracting oil from tar sands has several benefits.

Tar sands are mostly located in areas of central Canada that are rural and underdeveloped. The tar sands industry brings new residents, along with building projects and infrastructure, to these remote areas. Examples of projects supported and financed by the tar sands industry include new housing and improved local roads. Thanks to increasing populations and improving amenities such as new homes and better roads, the areas have become more appealing as places to live.

Extracting oil from the tar sands can be very profitable, and this benefits both the government and individuals. By collecting taxes from the oil companies, the government receives a certain percentage of the companies’ profits each year. When the industry is profitable, the government can collect billions of dollars in taxes. With all the money collected from oil companies, individuals’ taxes can remain low. Alberta, the Canadian province where the tar sands are located, has very low taxes on personal income and no tax on consumer goods.

Oil companies are investing in technologies to reduce the amount of carbon dioxide (CO2) released into the atmosphere during the extraction process. Extracting oil from tar sands requires considerable energy, currently generated by burning fossil fuels, which contributes to climate change by releasing CO2. However, one company has implemented carbon capture and storage—a process that captures CO2 and safely stores it underground. In a single year, carbon capture and storage prevented one million tons of CO2 from being released. The company using this technology has made their technique public, so other companies can now use the same methods to further reduce carbon emissions.

Listen to part of a lecture on the topic you just read about.

Actually, many experts oppose the extraction of oil from tar sands.

Here’s why. First, development.

Most people who’ve come to the tar sands are workers employed there.

But many of them don’t really live there permanently.

They simply work in the area for a few weeks at a time, and in between return to their families.

And in a different part of the country. That’s why much of the housing the industry is providing is only temporary.

For example, some workers stay in trailers, large vehicles on wheels that are easy to move.

And remember, when the oil runs out, the oil companies will leave.

And the new roads, well, after the companies leave, the roads won’t be maintained properly.

With poorly maintained roads and limited permanent housing, these areas won’t be very appealing.

Second, there’s a problem with depending on tar sands for tax revenue.

It’s more expensive to extract oil from tar sands than from other sources.

So, unlike other sources of energy, tar sands operations are profitable only when oil prices are high.

But oil prices rise and fall.

And when they fall, the tax revenue falls too.

For example, when the price of oil falls by just $1 per barrel, tax revenue in Alberta falls by over $200 million.

Well, if the government creates a budget based on expected revenue and that revenue drops unexpectedly, the government may not be able to pay for services citizens need.

Finally, yes, extraction companies are trying to reduce carbon emissions.

And they should, because the tar sands industry is one of Canada’s largest sources of carbon emissions.

But unfortunately, there’s another environmental problem.

Tar sands are transported in underground pipelines.

These pipelines can leak or spill oil, causing significant environmental damage, especially near water.

Tar sands are a thick, almost solid form of oil.

So unlike normal oil, which floats on top of water, tar sands oil sinks deep below the surface of the water, making it very difficult to remove.

From my perspective, just as Student Musk mentioned, it is a beneficial approach because optional attendance can be more flexible for university students who are always busy. Furthermore, in my opinion, optional attendance can also give students more opportunities to improve themselves in various ways because they will have more available time.

To be specific, instead of taking every class, students can learn knowledge at their own pace. For example, I am a medical student, and I need to acquire a lot of knowledge for my exams. While the teachers were always speaking slowly, the knowledge I learned from the lessons in school was not enough at all. As a result, I need to learn by myself through videos so that I can change the speaking speed of speakers. If I can choose not to go to every class session, I believe I can do better, and I can learn something that would not be taught in my school.

Some may argue that class attendance should not be optional, while it is true that class attendance policies can foster discipline and responsibility, this argument fails to consider that we can foster these abilities through other ways. For instance, students who choose not to attend the class need to study by themselves and pass the exams, which will also require strong discipline and responsibility.

Lecture 1

Our solar system has two types of planets in terms of their composition.

We have rocky planets like Earth, and we have gas giants like Uranus and Neptune that are composed mostly of gases like helium and hydrogen.

And there’s another interesting difference between gas giants and rocky planets.

The gas giants have more mass Than the rocky planets.

Lots more mass. When we talk about a planet’s mass, we’re basically talking about how strong its gravity is.

Uranus, which is the least massive of the gas giants, has about 14 times more mass than Earth.

And Earth is the most massive of the rocky planets.

There are no planets in our solar system with a mass between that of Earth and that of Uranus.

For a long time, researchers thought it wasn’t possible for planets to have a mass in between that of Earth and that of Uranus.

They reasoned that when our solar system was forming, Any developing planet with more mass and therefore more gravity than Earth would pull in a thick layer of hydrogen and helium, thus becoming a gas giant with even more mass.

That’s why when astronomers started looking for planets outside our solar system, we, which we call exoplanets, they didn’t expect to find any whose mass was between that of Earth and Uranus.

Ok, so when they discovered the first exoplanets, they calculated their mass.

They did this by observing slight gravitational effects of the exoplanets on the stars they orbited.

When a planet orbits a star, the planet’s gravity tugs very slightly on the star.

This tug causes the star to wobble, to move very slightly back and forth.

The more mass the planet has, the stronger it pulls on its star.

And by observing how much the star wobbles, Researchers can determine the planet’s mass.

And guess what? The first discovered exoplanets had Masses that fell in between Earth’s and Uranuses.

Surprise. And not only that. Of the thousands of exoplanets that have been discovered since then, Most are in this intermediate range of mass. Because of their mass, researchers call these planets super Earths.

But how much like Earth are they really? Are they rocky planets like Earth? And can they maybe support life? Or are they inhospitable gas giants? Mass alone doesn’t tell us a planet’s composition.

For that, it helps to know the planet’s density, which we can calculate if we know the planet’s mass and its size, its diameter. And here again, the stars can help us.

When a planet passes in front of a star, it blocks some of the light coming from the star, and we can gauge how large the planet is by based on how much of the star’s light it blocks.

We can get additional clues about the planet’s composition.

By analyzing the way light passes through its atmosphere.

Armed with this kind of information, researchers have determined that super Earths up to twice the size of Earth seem to be rocky, while larger ones are probably gas giants.

As for supporting life, since super Earths have more mass.and therefore stronger gravity than Earth has, the rocky ones might be able to hang on to a thick atmosphere Thicker than ours, which would keep heat in.

That means that some might support life. Even if they’re farther from their star than Earth is from our sun.

Also, if rocky super Earths are more massive than Earth, they’d also probably have a smoother surface. So instead of deep oceans and vast continents like Earth, they might have shallow seas and lots of island chains.

And here on Earth, at least, island chains in shallow seas tend to support diverse life forms.

But here’s another. If super Earths are so common, shouldn’t our solar system have one, too?Some speculate that maybe our system once had one. Or even that there’s one out there that we haven’t detected yet.

There are some good arguments for that, too. Either way, a super Earth and our solar system would mean we, our solar system is more normal, more like all those other systems out there, which I think would be good. Because if our solar system Is incredibly special and rare, that could mean that the conditions that enabled life to develop here are also rare. So, personally, I’d much rather our solar system be normal.

阅读 Spectroscopy and the Substance of Stars

strengthening

Spectroscopy involves the analysis of light from a star (or anything else) to provide information about what the object emitting the light, or a gas that is absorbing the light, is made of. The name spectroscopy comes from "spectrum"-- the familiar pattern of colored light that you see when white light is passed through a prism (or that you see in a rainbow itself). When the rainbow pattern produced by light sent through a prism is magnified, it turns out that there are many sharp lines in the spectrum–these lines can be dark or bright. The first person to notice this, early in the nineteenth century, was an English physicist and chemist, William Wollaston, who passed light from the Sun through a prism and saw many dark lines in the magnified spectrum. Shortly after Wollaston’s investigation, the German physicist Josef von Fraunhofer also noticed the dark lines in the spectrum of the Sun, which he studied in the second decade of the nineteenth century.

The next key developments were made in Germany by Robert Bunsen and Gustav Kirchhoff in the 1850s and 1860s. This was the same Robert Bunsen associated with the famous piece of laboratory equipment, the Bunsen burner. But the link between Bunsen and the burner is important and relevant because the spectra that Bunsen and Kirchhoff studied were obtained by heating different substances in the clear flame of a Bunsen burner and then analyzing the light they emitted using spectroscopy.

In the spectrum of light from the Sun or a star, the dark lines show up in profusion, some thinner and fainter, others thicker and darker. Fraunhofer counted 574 lines in the spectrum of light from the Sun, each at its own precisely determined wavelength, and found many of the same lines in light from Venus (which is simply reflected sunlight, so this is not very surprising) and from many stars (which is much more significant, since they shine by their own light). The pattern of lines is unique to each light-emitting object. The key discovery made by Bunsen, and followed up by Kirchhoff, was that each element produces its own characteristic set of lines in the spectrum, as distinctive and unmistakable as a fingerprint. When the substance is hot, it produces bright lines of emission; when white light is passed through a cold gas, the result is a spectrum in which there are dark lines of absorption. But for a particular gas (say, hydrogen), the bright lines produced when the gas is hot are in exactly the same places in the spectrum (that is, at exactly the same wavelengths) as the dark lines seen when white light passes through the gas when it is cold.

The distinctive orange light seen in street lamps, for example, is caused by a trace of sodium in the tubes of the lights that has been energized by the electric current flowing through the tube. Hot sodium always radiates energy at two well-defined wavelengths in the yellow-orange part of the spectrum, producing two bright yellow-orange lines in the spectrum. This is a particularly appropriate example, since in 1859 Kirchhoff made the first identification of the presence of any element outside Earth when he found the characteristic sodium lines (in this case, as dark lines of absorption) in the spectrum of light from the Sun.

Once the relationship between the chemical composition of a substance and its spectrum was appreciated, and once chemists had studied many different substances in this way in the laboratory by using the heat of Bunsen burners to take the spectroscopic fingerprints of different elements, they could immediately (as the example of the discovery of sodium in the Sun highlights) identify which elements were present in the Sun and stars by identifying which spectral lines were seen in the light from those stars–provided the stars were bright enough for their spectra to be studied in this way. They could use this tool to find out what stars were made of.

Lecture 2

You see, tipi rings are critical indicators.

They provide direct evidence of domestic, economic and nomadic life.

They help us figure out how these Native Americans, how these hunter-gatherer communities, how these lived more than 2,000 years ago, particularly their migration routes and patterns.

For example, of the thousands of tipi rings that have been found, the majority are in clusters, in groups of rings.

Most of the time, in a given cluster, some rings will be much larger than others.

The smaller ones were probably used as family residences as opposed to larger ones.

Presumably, the large teepees were used as community gathering places.

For one study researchers visited tipi ring sites in the Great Plains states of Montana and Wyoming.

There, they measured and mapped tipi rings in order to look for patterns.

How did they do this? First, for each stone, they measured its distance from the center of its ring and noted its position.

They used these measurements to create hand-drawn maps.

Um, it might interest you to know that archaeology students did the measuring and mapping.

Many traditional hands on archaeological methods like this have pretty much been replaced by technology, though, like aerial digital photography.

But I do not consider hand mapping, this type of field research to be a waste of time.

After all, technology is not always available or affordable.

And who knows what you might discover by combining the results of old and new methods.

In fact, this particular study did just that.

In addition to analyzing students maps, researchers used a Global Positioning System or gps.

They used images from GPS satellites to document the precise location coordinates of of individual stones and tipi rings.

The researchers also used a second technology, Geographic Information Systems, or gis.

GIS is different. It produces a sort of three dimensional model of a larger area’s physical characteristics.

So while GPS shows where each stone is on a two dimensional plane, GIS shows the assemblages in 3D.

The students maps meanwhile, provide ground level details that cannot be captured by GPS or gis.

Researchers used all these data to draw conclusions about the inhabitants of the teepees.

For example, teepees with a four pole frame are usually circular at the bottom.

Those with a three pole frame have a more oval shaped bottom.

So since we know which tribes used four pole frames and which used three poles, we can figure out which tribe lived in which area by looking at the shape of the tipi rings.

In this study, the rings were determined to be more circular, suggesting that maybe the Crow, the Shoshone or the Blackfeet tribe occupied that area in prehistoric times.

And that’s not the only thing researchers learned.

Within many of the tipi rings, there was evidence of cooking hearths.

The remains of burnt charcoal in the hearths were used to date some of the teepee rings.

These dates revealed that the teepees in different areas had been occupied one after another in succession, instead of at the same time.

This suggests that people migrated from one area to the other.

First, the reading mentions that harmful greenhouse gases are emitted from fossil fuels, which are burned during the process of single-use plastic water bottle production. Besides, most plastic water bottles are rarely recycled, so they finally poison animals and damage the environment. However, the speaker disputes this theory by demonstrating that not only are the water bottles made of plastic, but also other drinks’ containers are made of plastic, and they are fatter than plastic water bottles. Second, according to the reading, single-use plastic water bottles are harmful to people’s health because the water inside them is not strictly regulated. Finally, the reading article declares that choosing alternative water sources, such as free public water fountains, can cause potential financial savings for consumers. Nevertheless, the speaker offers a counterargument by illustrating an example that people choose to go to the neighboring town to buy water when their town banned the sale of water in plastic bottles. Consequently, their town raises the price of other products to compensate for the lost profit, so people can not save money in fact.

阅读

In the United States, people buy billions of single-use plastic water bottles every year, and most of these bottles are never recycled. Some universities, national parks, and cities in the United States recently banned (prohibited) the sale of water in plastic bottles. Supporters argue that there are several important reasons why more places should ban single-use plastic water bottles.

Environment: One reason is to protect the environment. Large amounts of fossil fuels (oil and natural gas) are burned to produce plastic for water bottles. The burning of fossil fuels emits harmful greenhouse gases, such as carbon dioxide, into the atmosphere. Additionally, since plastic water bottles are rarely recycled, most of them end up in landfills or in the oceans, where they poison animals and damage the environment. Therefore, banning plastic water bottles will help preserve the environment by reducing harmful emissions and waste.

Health: Another reason for banning them is people’s health. In the United States, tap water that people drink at home is strictly regulated by a government agency, but there are no such stringent regulations for water sold in plastic bottles. Water bottles are made of plastic that may contain toxic chemicals. The longer water bottles are stored, the more likely the chemicals will start to escape into the water, which may result in water contamination. Therefore, banning plastic water bottles will be beneficial for people’s health.

Money Savings: A final reason is related to potential financial savings for consumers. If purchased on a regular basis, bottled water is expensive, and alternative water sources, such as public water fountains, are free of charge. For example, local governments in New York and San Francisco are planning to install even more water fountains in public places. Researchers have calculated that, by using alternative water sources, an average American consumer may save up to $1,000 per year.

听力

Unfortunately, it’s unlikely that many places will ban the sale of single use plastic water bottles anytime soon.

Here’s first,

it’s doubtful that banning only plastic water bottles will help significantly reduce harmful emissions or waste.

You see, besides water, many other beverages are sold in plastic containers because many beverages other than water are carbonated.

You know, they have tiny bubbles that people like in their drinks.

They require much thicker and stronger plastic containers.

This means that much more plastic is needed for their production.

By contrast, companies are now producing even thinner plastic water bottles and are using less and less plastic.

So among all plastic containers, water bottles do the least damage to the environment and banning only them will not help much.

Second, if people can drink tap water at home, that’s definitely better for their health.

But the issue is that people drink a lot of water on the go rather than at home.

Research has shown that when plastic water bottles are not available, people tend to consume more unhealthy drinks such as sodas and juices.

Most sodas and juices contain high amounts of sugar and calories, while water has none of those.

So if plastic water bottles are banned, people will likely consume more sugary high calorie drinks, which may negatively affect their health.

Finally, the money savings probably will not be substantial.

Let me show you why one small town in the United States recently banned the sale of bottled water and what happened next.

Well, consumers who still wanted to buy bottled water went out of town and shopped in neighboring areas where there was no such ban.

The small businesses located in the town, such as grocery stores and coffee shops, lost profits from those customers.

The small businesses then considered increasing prices on other products in order to compensate for their losses.

With the increased prices on other products, consumers would not save much money.

But the link between Bunsen and the burner is important and relevant because the spectra that Bunsen and Kirchhoff studied were obtained by heating different substances in the clear flame of a Bunsen burner and then analyzing the light they emitted using spectroscopy.

In the spectrum of light from the Sun or a star, the dark lines show up in profusion, some thinner and fainter, others thicker and darker. Fraunhofer counted 574 lines in the spectrum of light from the Sun, each at its own precisely determined wavelength, and found many of the same lines in light from Venus (which is simply reflected sunlight, so this is not very surprising) and from many stars (which is much more significant, since they shine by their own light). The pattern of lines is unique to each light-emitting object. The key discovery made by Bunsen, and followed up by Kirchhoff, was that each element produces its own characteristic set of lines in the spectrum, as distinctive and unmistakable as a fingerprint. When the substance is hot, it produces bright lines of emission; when white light is passed through a cold gas, the result is a spectrum in which there are dark lines of absorption. But for a particular gas (say, hydrogen), the bright lines produced when the gas is hot are in exactly the same places in the spectrum (that is, at exactly the same wavelengths) as the dark lines seen when white light passes through the gas when it is cold.

The distinctive orange light seen in street lamps, for example, is caused by a trace of sodium in the tubes of the lights that has been energized by the electric current flowing through the tube. Hot sodium always radiates energy at two well-defined wavelengths in the yellow-orange part of the spectrum, producing two bright yellow-orange lines in the spectrum. This is a particularly appropriate example, since in 1859 Kirchhoff made the first identification of the presence of any element outside Earth when he found the characteristic sodium lines (in this case, as dark lines of absorption) in the spectrum of light from the Sun.

Once the relationship between the chemical composition of a substance and its spectrum was appreciated, and once chemists had studied many different substances in this way in the laboratory by using the heat of Bunsen burners to take the spectroscopic fingerprints of different elements, they could immediately (as the example of the discovery of sodium in the Sun highlights) identify which elements were present in the Sun and stars by identifying which spectral lines were seen in the light from those stars–provided the stars were bright enough for their spectra to be studied in this way. They could use this tool to find out what stars were made of.

Lecture 3

Listen to a lecture in an astronomy class.

Imagine you’re observing a rocky planet, say, Earth, from a distance, from a fixed location in space.

And you want to know how long it takes for that planet to make one full rotation around its axis.

How could you figure this out, Brandon?

I guess you could look for a feature, something large, like a mountain chain, and track it, you know, see how much time it takes for the feature to reappear in the same position.

Good for rocky planets like Earth.

If a distinct feature keeps appearing on schedule, if it rotates with regularity, this allows us to measure the rotational speed with great precision.

But what about planets with a different composition, like the gas giants Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune?

Would this same method work? Probably not.

I mean, if you observed these planets from a distance, you wouldn’t see any solid surface features, right?

You’d only see an atmosphere of thick clouds.

We believe they have a small solid core of rock and ice, but we can’t see the core through the atmosphere, an atmosphere that’s constantly subjected to high winds.

So if all we could see from our fixed point in space are the planet’s swirling clouds, and it would be difficult to find a distinct feature and clock its rotation.

So then what else could we do?

Well, back in the 1950s, when the first radio telescopes were available, we discovered radio signals coming from Jupiter.

They were emitted by Jupiter’s magnetic field, which is linked to the rotation of the planet’s inner core.

We realized that we could use these radio signals to determine Jupiter’s rotational period, the time it takes to complete each rotation.

However, we couldn’t detect radio signals from the other, more distant gas giants.

Fast forward about 30 years to the Voyager missions.

The Voyager spacecrafts were able to collect radio signals from those gas giants, including Saturn.

Based on these data, Saturn’s rotational period was calculated to be 10 hours and 39 minutes.

So after the Voyager missions, we thought we had a good handle on how to measure the rotation rates of the outer gas giants.

But then, 15 years later, Cassini made a puzzling discovery.

Cassini is a probe, a spacecraft that orbited Saturn.

Based on radio data Cassini sent back to Earth, it seemed that Saturn’s rotational period had changed by about 1%.

The period was about six minutes longer since Voyager had measured it.

This suggests that radio signals emitted from the magnetic field might not reflect a gas planet’s internal rotation as precisely as we had thought.

But why couldn’t both readings be accurate?

Can’t a planet’s rotation speed change?

Not if we consider Saturn’s immensity.

A celestial body this large cannot really change its rotation in such a short span of time.

And the magnetic fields being pulled along by the planet’s rotating core.

But something was slowing down Saturn’s magnetic field.

Solar wind, perhaps. And made the magnetic field lag behind.

Okay, so if the radio signals method isn’t reliable, what else can be done?

A planetary scientist who decided to verify Neptune’s rotation rate, Eric Karkoschka, Might have found an answer.

Karkoshka spent countless hours examining hundreds of images of Neptune taken over the past 20 years.

Most were taken by the Hubble Space Telescope.

And during Karkoshka’s painstaking research, he identified several distinct features, including two cloud formations that stood out in Neptune’s atmosphere.

He tracked these cloud formations through the various images and noticed that they reappeared exactly on schedule.

In other words, they rotate with incredible regularity.

Isn’t it similar to the method we said we used for rocky planets?

Right. But with the help of images instead of direct observations.

And based on this research, Karkoshka calculated that one day on Neptune is slightly less than 16 hours.

Now, you might ask yourself, who cares about a gas planet’s rotation?

Why would Karkoshka spend so much time on this?

The reason is that a planet’s rotation is one of its most basic attributes.

If we can accurately determine its rotation speed, we can learn many other things about the planet.

For example, we know Neptune’s mass, but we’re not certain how it’s distributed.

Knowing Neptune’s rotational period can offer clues to this and other mysteries.

阅读 Cave Artists

The earliest surviving cave and rock art was created in the Paleolithic period (40,000- 10,000 years ago) in locations that were not sites of human habitation. Some Paleolithic artwork was ephemeral-only six examples of open-air engravings survive-but the fine-art engravings and paintings that decorate caves were made to last and did last, in some cases for hundreds and even thousands of years, during which they were available for delight and use. Big cave galleries thus contained work done over a long period, available for comparison to people who had some notion of historical time and were developing a sense of their ancestry. The best Paleolithic art, especially the polychrome paintings, was the work of professionals.

We can say this with some confidence, for cave art at its best was difficult and expensive to produce. In the first place, it required lighting. Some 85 certain and 31 probable examples of Paleolithic lamps have survived, but less than one-third of them were found inside caves. The conjecture, therefore, is that artists usually worked by torchlight. Both lamps and torches consume animal fats in large quantities. Second, while it is true that some of the best cave paintings, especially at Altamira in Spain, were painted by artists standing up or in some cases lying down or squatting, others required elaborate scaffolding, no different in principle from that used by Renaissance artist Michelangelo when he painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel. Some of the paintings were done on a gigantic scale or at heights many feet above the cave floor. The sheer scale of the art is daunting. The big cave vault at Lascaux, known as the Picture Gallery, is over 100 feet long and 35 feet wide. Caves were especially chosen for their size as well as for their security. Niaux in the Pyrenees Mountains in Europe is over half a mile in length, and this is by no means unusual. The big caveat Rouffignac runs over 6 miles (more than 9 kilometers) into the mountain, and some of its huge collection of drawing-engravings are nearly 7 feet (over 2 meters) long.

Professional cave artists, then, needed not only platforms and scaffolding, whose existence at Lascaux, for instance, is betrayed by sockets cut into the walls, but assistants. [A] They mixed the paints, some of which had to be used quickly before they dried; filled the lamps or held the torches; put up and secured the scaffolding; and made the brushes from twigs, feathers, leaves, and animal hairs, to the satisfaction of the master. [B] These assistants probably graduated into masters themselves. [C] It is not going too far to speak of a studio system as the basis of Paleolithic cave art. [D] After all, there is positive evidence that art studios, where important works were fabricated and artists trained, existed in Egypt at least as far back as 3000 B.C. That still leaves a gap of 7,000 years from the end of the Paleolithic period, but the quality and consistency of the best painted work in caves, and the evidence of the time, expense, and skill required to produce them, does suggest that artists needed the collective support of something very like a studio. The probability is that the leading cave artists were important persons.

This brings us to quality. To modern eyes, accustomed to 5,000 years of continuous development in the depiction of living forms, the best of the Paleolithic paintings are magnificent. Indeed, seen in depth and in the total silence of the caves, the images are awesome. Human forms are rare and often quite unsophisticated,but the variety of animal forms is impressive. In the eight galleries of the great cave at Les Eyzies, there are multiple examples of mammoths, reindeer, horses, stags, bison, and wolves, as well as humanoids and abstractions or signs. These interlocking galleries,unfolding one by one, are meant to impress and they do. The art is ,both detailed and monumental, oscillating designedly between simplification and elaboration, between stasis and extreme dynamism. Some Paleolithic artists clearly understood both the anatomy of the animals they depicted and their principles of motion, the result of intense observation over many years and of a self-discipline in rendering that suggests a long apprenticeship and extensive study.

Emma? Well, ships. As a ship moves through water, drag is the force of the water pulling on it, slowing it down, and it’s affected by how fast the ship is going.

Plus other things like what kind of a surface it has.

But if, say, it’s covered in barnacles or other marine organisms, that increases drag.

Don’t laugh. Some engineers have beaten you to that idea, looking along the lines of covering the surface of the hull, the bottom of the ship, or part of it in small ridges.

But you have me thinking of some other work in this area.

So first note that cutting down drag even a little bit has a big impact on the fuel efficiency of a ship.

Even a 10% reduction would be considered terrific.

One approach that’s been tried is releasing air bubbles close to the hull while the ship is moving.

This creates a partial barrier of air, of gas, between the water and the ship’s surface, which reduces the water’s pull on the ship.

Reduces, but certainly doesn’t eliminate.

Okay, well, now imagine an object completely encased in a bubble that’s falling through water.

The water doesn’t touch the object at all, right?

So the drag is way reduced.

Now, this had first been conceived of over 200 years ago, but how do you get an object into a bubble and keep it there while it’s moving through water?

Well, now it’s been done using two different methods.

In one, a metal ball about 2cm in diameter was heated up to about 400 degrees Celsius.

Meanwhile, water in a deep tank was heated to 95 degrees Celsius, just 5 degrees under the boiling point of water.

When the super-hot ball was dropped into the water right away, it boiled the water immediately around it, which created a layer of vapor.

The speed of the ball and the water temperature had to be just right.

But when it was the ball became completely surrounded by gas due to what’s called the Leidenfrost effect.

This phenomenon was described in 1796 by the German scientist Johann Leidenfrost.

And you’ve seen it at work in everyday life.

Imagine you heat up a frying pan, then sprinkle some drops of water onto it.

Each water droplet quickly moves, skitters around the pan, right?

That’s because the heat has caused a layer of vapor to form beneath the droplets, separating them from the pan’s surface.

So there’s hardly any friction, hardly any drag.

Similarly, this metal ball sinking in the water encountered very little drag there in its bubble.

Now, the other method of achieving that bubble effect uses a superhydrophobic coating.

Hydrophobic means water avoiding.

The material in that can creates a hydrophobic coating so that if it rains, the water just forms droplets and rolls off.

So superhydrophobic substances do this to an even greater extent.

The researchers sprayed the metal ball with the superhydrophobic coating, which essentially creates a layer of gas between the ball and the water.

And it did this at room temperature, which, as you can imagine, is attractive for potential practical applications.

Ships don’t travel through boiling water right now.

Task 4

Now, you may have noticed that different animals eyes have different appearances. Why? It’s interesting actually. You see, based on the kind of food and animal eats and how it gets that food, the animal has different needs in terms of eyesight and what it needs to see. And so over time, the structure of animals eyes has evolved. Specifically the shape of their pupils. You know, the dark areas in the center of the eye, animals pupil shape has evolved to provide them with a kind of eyesight that’s most beneficial for their particular survival needs.

So many predators need eyesight that allows them to judge distance accurately. This is important for their survival because they rely on hunting. They hunt their prey by hiding, waiting, watching it move. So these predators have eyes that allow them to focus on their prey and see it clearly in front of them. The eye is structured such that the center of their vision is sharp, and this helps them to accurately measure the distance at which their prey is located.

So a snake. Its pupils are narrow and go up and down. Having vertical pupils allows the snake to focus completely on what’s in front of it. Say a mouse, and to judge exactly when the mouse is close enough to catch.

But then prey animals, which need to avoid predators to survive their eyes have evolved differently. Many prey animals are herbivores and spend a lot of time in open areas grazing on plants. This can make herbivores vulnerable, since predators could come at them from all directions while they eat. So yeah, they don’t need eyes that let them see their food source in front of them. They need eyes that expand their vision on either side so they can detect danger around them.

Take goats. Goats have horizontal pupils that extend sideways from left to right, and these horizontal pupils give them a wide view of the field of grass they’re standing in. So when their heads are down and they’re eating grass, they can easily see any predators there may be in the field.

作文

We can learn from the reading that beavers make dams that block the flow of water. Three benefits are proposed in the reading regarding its promotion, while all of them are refuted by the lecture, which states that all these benefits have flaws and none can be definitively proven.

First, the reading mentions that beaver dams increase available water to communities because they can not only slow down the river and keep a lot of water in the area, but also allow water to seep down into the soil and spread. However, the speaker disputes this theory by demonstrating that they may cause flooding by blocking the culverts, which are special tunnels built underneath the roads or railroads that cross streams or small rivers. As a result, the water in the culverts floods above the road and damages the roadway and even nearby houses.

Second, according to the reading, beaver dams increase biodiversity because they can help to store and retain water, which can nurture more vegetation and attract wildlife. While the speaker agrees with the reading that beaver dams may increase overall biodiversity, she argues that they harm some types of organisms. In fact, beavers built dams with wood, which was obtained by chewing through tree trunks. Furthermore, the dams can harm even more trees by changing course slightly, forming beaver ponds, which cause trees’ death by covering the roots of trees with water for a long time.

Finally, although the speaker acknowledges the validity of the reading’s point that beaver dams’ slow-moving water and relatively stable temperature provide an ideal habitat for some kinds of fish, she presents a contrasting argument that beaver dams may harm fish by creating a barrier that prevents fish from traveling forward. To be specific, dams usually have passageways between branches, through which fish can get stuck behind dams if the force of the water isn’t strong enough to push them through. Moreover, dams also increase the accumulation of sediment or dirt particles which is especially harmful to young fish.

阅读

Beavers are medium-sized mammals that inhabit rivers and streams throughout North America and parts of South America and Europe. They are best known for building dams, or structures made of twigs and branches that block the flow of water. Beaver dams provide numerous benefits to both people and the environment; as a result, efforts are being made to increase the beaver population in many areas.

One of the benefits of beaver dams is that they increase the amount of water available to communities. Without dams, water would flow through rivers without stopping. Dams create a barrier in the river that slows the flow of water and keeps large quantities of it in the area. Not only do dams keep rivers full, they also allow water to seep down into the soil, penetrating land far away from the river bed. This increases the water supply for both townspeople and farmers, something which is especially important in times of drought.

Second, beaver dams significantly increase biodiversity (the variety of plants and animals) in the areas where they are located. Because dams help to store and retain water, there will be more vegetation, including grass, shrubs, and other plants alongside rivers with dams. Wildlife in turn are attracted by the vegetation, which provides food, shelter, and other benefits for a number of species, including birds, elk, and deer.

Finally, beaver dams can turn a river into an ideal habitat for certain types of fish. Since the water that accumulates behind a dam flows very slowly compared to water in other parts of the river, fish that prefer slow-moving water can inhabit rivers where there are beaver dams. This slow-moving water also provides a protective habitat for fish during the winter due to its relatively stable temperature.

听力

Now listen to part of a lecture on the topic you just read about.

Although most scientists agree that beaver dams can be beneficial, they’re also known to cause certain problems.

So officials need to take precautions when introducing beavers into new areas.

First, beaver dams do increase local water supplies, but they sometimes also cause flooding.

You see, beavers often build dams in front of culverts.

Culverts are special tunnels built beneath roads or railroads.

In places where the roads or railroads cross streams or small rivers, culverts allow the flow of water to pass underneath the road.

But when a beaver dam blocks a culvert, water cannot flow through the tunnel and may flood the road above, damaging the roadway and even nearby houses.

Second, beaver dams may increase overall biodiversity, but some types of organisms, especially trees, can be harmed by them in a couple of ways.

Beavers harm some trees by chewing through their trunks and then using the wood to build dams.

Once built, the dams themselves can harm even more trees because beaver dams cause water in rivers and streams to change course slightly, forming pools known as beaver ponds on previously dried land.

These newly formed ponds can cover the roots of trees with water, and trees whose roots remain underwater too long will die.

Finally, it’s true that beaver dams can benefit fish.

However, this isn’t always the case.

One way beaver dams may harm fish is by creating a barrier that prevents fish from traveling forward.

Dams usually have passageways between branches.

However, fish can get stuck behind dams if the force of the water isn’t strong enough to push them through.

And because dams block water flow, they also increase the accumulation of sediment or dirt particles in the slow moving water behind the dam, making the water dirty, something that is especially harmful to young fish.

精读 Cave Artists

The earliest surviving cave and rock art was created in the Paleolithic period (40,000- 10,000 years ago) in locations that were not sites of human habitation. Some Paleolithic artwork was ephemeral——only six examples of open-air engravings survive—but the fine-art engravings and paintings that decorate caves were made to last and did last, in some cases for hundreds and even thousands of years, during which they were available for delight and use. Big cave galleries thus contained work done over a long period, available for comparison to people who had some notion of historical time and were developing a sense of their ancestry. The best Paleolithic art, especially the polychrome paintings, was the work of professionals.

We can say this with some confidence, for cave art at its best was difficult and expensive to produce. In the first place, it required lighting. Some 85 certain and 31 probable examples of Paleolithic lamps have survived, but less than one-third of them were found inside caves. The conjecture, therefore, is that artists usually worked by torchlight. Both lamps and torches consume animal fats in large quantities. Second, while it is true that some of the best cave paintings, especially at Altamira in Spain, were painted by artists standing up or in some cases lying down or squatting, others required elaborate scaffolding, no different in principle from that used by Renaissance artist Michelangelo when he painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel. Some of the paintings were done on a gigantic scale or at heights many feet above the cave floor. The sheer scale of the art is daunting. The big cave vault at Lascaux, known as the Picture Gallery, is over 100 feet long and 35 feet wide. Caves were especially chosen for their size as well as for their security. Niaux in the Pyrenees Mountains in Europe is over half a mile in length, and this is by no means unusual. The big caveat Rouffignac runs over 6 miles (more than 9 kilometers) into the mountain, and some of its huge collection of drawing-engravings are nearly 7 feet (over 2 meters) long.

In the second place, much like the painting on the Sistine Chapel ceiling, some great cave art appears on surfaces that could have been reached only by using complicated scaffolding.

Professional cave artists, then, needed not only platforms and scaffolding, whose existence at Lascaux, for instance, is betrayed by sockets cut into the walls, but assistants. [A] They mixed the paints, some of which had to be used quickly before they dried; filled the lamps or held the torches; put up and secured the scaffolding; and made the brushes from twigs, feathers, leaves, and animal hairs, to the satisfaction of the master. Without assistants to perform these needed tasks, cave artists would have been unable to create large and difficult-to-reach paintings. These assistants probably graduated into masters themselves. [C] It is not going too far to speak of a studio system as the basis of Paleolithic cave art. [D] After all, there is positive evidence that art studios, where important works were fabricated and artists trained, existed in Egypt at least as far back as 3000 B.C. That still leaves a gap of 7,000 years from the end of the Paleolithic period, but the quality and consistency of the best painted work in caves, and the evidence of the time, expense, and skill required to produce them, does suggest that artists needed the collective support of something very like a studio. The probability is that the leading cave artists were important persons.

This brings us to quality. To modern eyes, accustomed to 5,000 years of continuous development in the depiction of living forms, the best of the Paleolithic paintings are magnificent. Indeed, seen in depth and in the total silence of the caves, the images are awesome. Human forms are rare and often quite unsophisticated,but the variety of animal forms is impressive. In the eight galleries of the great cave at Les Eyzies, there are multiple examples of mammoths, reindeer, horses, stags, bison, and wolves, as well as humanoids and abstractions or signs. These interlocking galleries,unfolding one by one, are meant to impress and they do. The art is ,both detailed and monumental, oscillating designedly between simplification and elaboration, between stasis and extreme dynamism. Some Paleolithic artists clearly understood both the anatomy of the animals they depicted and their principles of motion, the result of intense observation over many years and of a self-discipline in rendering that suggests a long apprenticeship and extensive study.

A. Open-air engravings were made without an artistic or historical sense, and consequently were not meant to last through the ages.

B. The work must have involved the collaboration of assistants who became apprentices to the master and eventually produced art of their own.

C. Evidence suggests that the art studio system of the Paleolithic appears to have served as the basis for the art studio system of Egypt.

D. The sheer size of cave art and the nature of the environment required artists to use platforms, scaffolding, and torches.

E. Assistants made the paints, built the scaffolding and a variety of tools, and obtained the models for their masters.

F. The high-quality depiction of animal forms reveals careful observation of their anatomy and knowledge of the principles of motion.

阅读 Chimpanzee Communication

Do animals communicate deliberately, meaning do they communicate with a goal in mind? It would help if we could ask them what they intended to communicate and they could reply using communication signals that we could understand. To achieve such twoway communication, humans must either learn to use the communication signals of the species we wish to study or teach an animal to use some form of human language. Since we have not yet been successful in understanding more than rudimentary aspects of animal communication signals, the latter has presented itself as the best option. Apes have been taught to communicate with humans using American Sign Language or by pointing to symbols that represent words. They have not been taught verbal communication using spoken language because the vocal apparatus of apes is very different from that of humans and does not allow them to make the same vocalizations that we do.

Allen and Beatrix Gardner trained several chimpanzees to communicate with humans using American Sign Language, beginning in 1966 with a chimpanzee called Washoe. The chimpanzees learned to use signs to refer to objects and individuals, and all of them acquired vocabularies that allowed them to express requests, such as "Ice cream hurry give me." By the chimpanzees’ frustrated behavior when these requests were not honored, compared with when they were, it was clear that these were deliberate forms of communication. The chimpanzees also announced when the next activity in the daily routine should occur. This announcement of a pending event is an aspect of awareness of the future that indicates deliberate communication. Emotion entered into the signingmore emotive events evoked more signing-but cognition was obviously a major aspect of their communication.

To convince critics that the chimpanzees were expressing genuine requests and were coming up with answers to questions by use of their own powers of cognition, it was necessary for the Gardners to prove that the chimpanzees were not using subtle cues given inadvertently by the humans caring for them. By responding to cues produced by the humans in their presence, the apes could appear to be communicating intelligently and deliberately but would merely be performing some sort of clever mimicry. In other words, they might be similar to Clever Hans, the horse that was once thought to be able to read numbers written on a board and to count them out by tapping his foot on the ground. Later it was found that the horse used subtle cues that his owner supplied unknowingly, such as the blink of an eyelid when the horse tapped the required number of times. Clever Hans could not perform the task when his owner was not present.

To test whether a similar use of cues might be occurring with the chimpanzees, the Gardners designed an experiment in which the chimpanzees had to name objects shown to them on a video monitor. Their responses were recorded by a human who could not see the screen and did not know what the chimpanzees were observing. In fact, there was no human who knew what was on the screen present in the room with the chimpanzees. In this controlled experiment, the chimpanzees were able to name objects accurately. Therefore, their use of sign language was self- generated and not some form of mimicry or associative learning.

The chimpanzees also used the sign language they had learned to tell humans things they did not already know. For example, when very young, Washoe dropped one of her toys into a hole in the inside wall of the caravan in which she lived. That night, when Allen Gardner visited her, she attracted his attention to a part of the wall below the hole and signed "Open, open" many times over. From this communication Allen deduced what had happened and retrieved the toy. Washoe had used sign language to communicate something really new to a human. This shows genuine communication, communication made deliberately. Again, there was no question of the chimpanzee’s having communicated merely by reading subtle cues given by a human.

Lecture 6

Listen to part of a lecture in an anthropology class.

Traditionally, anthropologists studied rituals and ritual behaviors in the context of pre-modern and non-modern cultures.

But recently we’ve begun paying more attention to rituals in contemporary cultures.

And it appears that rituals have both changed and stayed the same.

So what makes a ritual?

First, there’s formality.

Rituals are not relaxed affairs.

Think of the Olympic medal ceremony, for example.

That’s something that existed in ancient Greece and continues today.

The content of the ritual has certainly changed, but the ritual is still an extremely formal event.

Why do I say that, Brittany?

Oh, I don’t know about ancient Greece, but today the winning athletes have to stand in a certain order on those platforms in a national anthems played and flags are raised, the athletes bow and the medal is placed around their neck. Kind of like a play, really like a play.

Different actors, but the same stage directions every single time.

Which brings me to a second defining aspect of ritual, what’s called invariance.

So invariance, because rituals aren’t only formal, they’re also carried out in the same way every time.

No matter how much the world changes, Ritual is steadfast, predictable, and there’s comfort in that.

The gold medalist always stands on the highest platform.

They always play the national anthem of the gold medalist’s home country, and so on.

And because the medal ceremony has been consistent, invariant for over 100 years, each one creates a tie to all the medal ceremonies that came before it.

This connection to the past is very attractive to people.

Okay. The third element we associate with rituals is what we call sacral symbolism.

Sacral symbolism refers to images or objects or actions that communicate a special meaning, like a nation’s flag.

Since a flag can communicate many emotions and meanings, it’s more than a piece of cloth.

Plus, there may be rules about how to fold it, carry it, and so on.

So, like every morning before I leave my dorm room, I do the same things in the same order.

But I’ve always thought of them as habits.

Now, I’m wondering, are habits rituals?

That’s a good question, because there is an overlap between the definitions of habits and rituals.

For example, habits are often invariable, but they’re not formal or symbolic.

Yes, that’s the difference.

Say you stop by the same coffee shop every day on your way to school.

Now, if the coffee shop is just a convenient place to pick up coffee, or if you just happen to really like their coffee, then it’s a habit or routine.

But what if that visit takes on a symbolic meaning for you?

If you feel that your day must begin with a visit to this particular coffee shop, because it gives you a sense that this part of the day at least, is under your control.

And if the coffee shop were to go out of business, you’d feel a void, a sense that the world is random, arbitrary.

Then your visits to the coffee shop could qualify as ritual.

Now, most people wouldn’t consider something as commonplace as visiting a coffee shop a ritual, but I wanted to give you a sense that rituals can be personal, private as well as public.

Now, imagine how Olympic medalists would feel if the medal ceremonies were cancelled.

If the organizers announced, we’ll send you the medal in the mail, we’re skipping the ceremony this year.

I think they’d feel robbed of something important.

Agreed. And this tells us something important about rituals.

The end result, getting that cup of coffee or the Olympic medal isn’t what matters the most.

What really matters is the process, doing the ritual, going through the steps.

That’s why rituals remain a part of modern cultures.

So it may combine its existing skills or capabilities with those of another company to offer a new service together through what is known as a joint venture . The two companies create a third, separate company in a project or venture that joins their individual areas of expertise. The two original companies continue to operate independently at the same time that they run the new company together and share its profits.

For example, there is this news company, a television news company that wanted to start offering internet news. 精读 Chimpanzee Communication

Do animals communicate deliberately, meaning do they communicate with a goal in mind? It would help if we could ask them what they intended to communicate and they could reply using communication signals that we could understand. To achieve such twoway communication, humans must either learn to use the communication signals of the species we wish to study or teach an animal to use some form of human language. Since we have not yet been successful in understanding more than rudimentary aspects of animal communication signals, the latter has presented itself as the best option. Apes have been taught to communicate with humans using American Sign Language or by pointing to symbols that represent words. They have not been taught verbal communication using spoken language because the vocal apparatus of apes is very different from that of humans and does not allow them to make the same vocalizations that we do.

Allen and Beatrix Gardner trained several chimpanzees to communicate with humans using American Sign Language, beginning in 1966 with a chimpanzee called Washoe. The chimpanzees learned to use signs to refer to objects and individuals, and all of them acquired vocabularies that allowed them to express requests, such as "Ice cream hurry give me." By the chimpanzees’ frustrated behavior when these requests were not honored, compared with when they were, it was clear that these were deliberate forms of communication. The chimpanzees also announced when the next activity in the daily routine should occur. This announcement of a pending event is an aspect of awareness of the future that indicates deliberate communication. Emotion entered into the signing—more emotive events evoked more signing—but cognition was obviously a major aspect of their communication.

To convince critics that the chimpanzees were expressing genuine requests and were coming up with answers to questions by use of their own powers of cognition, it was necessary for the Gardners to prove that the chimpanzees were not using subtle cues given inadvertently by the humans caring for them. By responding to cues produced by the humans in their presence, the apes could appear to be communicating intelligently and deliberately but would merely be performing some sort of clever mimicry. In other words, they might be similar to Clever Hans, the horse that was once thought to be able to read numbers written on a board and to count them out by tapping his foot on the ground. Later it was found that the horse used subtle cues that his owner supplied unknowingly, such as the blink of an eyelid when the horse tapped the required number of times. Clever Hans could not perform the task when his owner was not present.

To test whether a similar use of cues might be occurring with the chimpanzees, the Gardners designed an experiment in which the chimpanzees had to name objects shown to them on a video monitor. Their responses were recorded by a human who could not see the screen and did not know what the chimpanzees were observing. In fact, there was no human who knew what was on the screen present in the room with the chimpanzees. In this controlled experiment, the chimpanzees were able to name objects accurately. Therefore, their use of sign language was self-generated and not some form of mimicry or associative learning.

The chimpanzees also used the sign language they had learned to tell humans things they did not already know. For example, when very young, Washoe dropped one of her toys into a hole in the inside wall of the caravan in which she lived. That night, when Allen Gardner visited her, she attracted his attention to a part of the wall below the hole and signed "Open, open" many times over. From this communication Allen deduced what had happened and retrieved the toy. Washoe had used sign language to communicate something really new to a human. This shows genuine communication, communication made deliberately. Again, there was no question of the chimpanzee’s having communicated merely by reading subtle cues given by a human.

Lecture 7

Listen to part of a lecture in an archaeology class.

So we’ve been speaking about archaeology in the Middle east, and now I’d like to look at a particular** site** that archaeologists have recently begun excavating.

Tells Eh Dawn. Tells Eh dawn was located in part of ancient Mesopotamia in what is now northern Syria.

Surveys of the site indicate that people lived at the site continuously for about 2,000 years, from approximately 6,000 BCE to 4,000 BCE.

Chronologically, the site spans three different major cultural periods.

One of those three is the Ubaiyid Culture.

Archaeologists have become increasingly interested in the Ubaid culture and Tellsay dawn represents a major opportunity for us to really study and understand this culture as it functioned in northern Mesopotamia.

You see, we’ve been forced to piece together most of our very limited knowledge of the Ubaid culture in this region from excavations at small village sized sites.

Some large centers of Ubaid culture do exist in the region, but they’re so heavily buried under deposits of sand and dirt that it’s been impossible to learn very much from them.

However, the information at Telsay dawn is close to the surface and it’s in a sizable site such as this one where we can learn the most about social organization, architecture, trade, things we archaeologists are very interested in.

So why all the particular attention on the Ubaid culture?

Well, I should tell you that for quite some time, the traditional view in archaeology has been that Middle Eastern civilization began down in southern Mesopotamia in what is now Iraq.

That’s where the Uruk culture thrived.

The consensus was that civilization began with the Uruk culture and spread north from there.

But that assumption was challenged by our increased knowledge of the Ubaid culture.

All the recent findings show the Ubaid culture to be a highly complex society.

At Tal Zay, dawn, we’re seeing evidence of some of the first local examples of the Ubaid’s use of irrigation in agriculture, the presence of regional centers, the construction of religious temples, and even monumental architecture.

And the Ubaid culture existed much earlier than the Uruk culture.

So it now appears that the advances in the Ubaid culture developed independently of the Uruk culture.

But now let’s go back to tell Zaydan.

There are a lot of discoveries that are broadening our understanding of life as it occurred there.

Consider an artifact from the Late Chalcolithic culture, for example.

Archaeologists found a stone seal among the Late Chalcolithic remnants.

It’s a large seal used for stamping items.

And there’s the symbol, the design of a deer carved on it.

The existence of this elaborate seal suggests that there were people in power, people able to restrict access to things by marking them with this seal, it shows us that society was beginning to split into different social classes.

This seal is very similar to another one that was found almost 300km away, suggesting the widespread emergence of a ruling class.

Artifacts also tell us that trade occurred at Tal Zeidan.

For example, we found that tar was obtained from the south for use in harvest tools.

Archaeologists have also found special blades made from volcanic rock, which was highly valued at that time.

The blades have the same unique physical characteristics and chemical composition of volcanic rock found on the shores of Lake Van, which is located about 400 km away in present day Turkey.

So definitely not a local product.

As for what comes next with this excavation, well, tell Zaydan, as I said earlier, is very large and so the process is going to take years.

But I think that one of the next logical steps is to really focus in on the transitions between the three cultures that occupy this site.

This is a rare opportunity.

As important as the Ubaid culture is, we shouldn’t limit ourselves to the Ubaid culture.

We’d benefit by looking closely at the interaction between these three cultures.

For example, were there peaceful cultural transitions, or were those transitions in fact marked by conflict?

作文

We can learn from the reading that a high-speed rail system will connect San Francisco and LA. Three benefits are proposed in the reading, while all of them are refuted by the lecture, which states that all these benefits have flaws and none can be definitively proven.

First, the reading mentions that maintaining roads is expensive, and the high-speed rail system can lead people to take the train instead of driving, so there will be less damage to the roads, and the budget for it can be reduced. However, the speaker disputes this theory by demonstrating that building the new system will cost more money than before. To be specific, the government needs to borrow 100 billion dollars for the high-speed rail system, which is 75 percent of the income tax collection. As a result, it will be a heavy burden, just like people will find it hard to pay back a loan that takes 75 percent of their income.

Second, according to the reading, traffic congestion is a serious problem. While the speaker agrees with the reading that the high-speed trains can relieve the congestion, she argues that people may not choose the high-speed trains in some places. In fact, public transportation is lacking in the urban areas, such as the West Coast. Since it is not a convenient choice to take high-speed trains because people cannot reach the station easily, people will keep driving, and it will not be helpful to lower the traffic congestion.

Finally, the reading declares that the high-speed train is the most environmentally friendly transportation form because it is more fuel efficient, which can reduce harmful fuel emissions. On the contrary, the speaker presents a contrasting argument that the fuel emissions will not be reduced as much as the Reading claims. Specifically, the new high-speed track will not be built for the whole route, and trains will slow down in the regular tracks to make the best use of available resources, which makes them less fuel efficient.

阅读

The United States currently has high-speed railway lines on the East Coast of the country. The East Coast high-speed trains have been very successful, and some experts believe that a similar high-speed rail system to connect the cities of San Francisco and Los Angeles in the state of California on the West Coast would have many benefits as well.

First, maintaining roads is expensive, and because of budget constraints, the state of California has had great difficulty in ensuring that the repairs needed to keep the roads in top condition are made. Advocates of the high-speed rail proposal point out that when people who would have driven to their destination take the train instead, there will be less damage to the roads. The amount of maintenance needed on roads will therefore decrease.

In addition, traffic congestion on one of the major roads between San Francisco and Los Angeles is already at record levels, and transportation experts predict that it will double over the next 25 years; clearly, this problem must be addressed. In some areas of the East Coast where traffic congestion has been a problem, high-speed trains have helped relieve the congestion, and they have become the most popular way to travel between some East Coast cities. A high-speed train between San Francisco and Los Angeles could become just as popular and could play a major role in helping to lower traffic congestion.

Finally, high-speed trains are one of the most environmentally friendly forms of transportation. Trains running at a high rate of speed are very fuel efficient: about five times more fuel efficient than cars and twice as efficient as regular trains. A high-speed rail line between San Francisco and Los Angeles could eliminate many billions of pounds of harmful fuel emissions produced by car engines and regular trains every year.

听力

The Reading makes high speed rail seem like a great choice for California, but it’s not.

The benefits would be much less substantial than the reading suggests.

First, it’s true that the state of California would save some money on road maintenance, but you have to compare that to the money California would have to spend on building the high speed rail.

To build a new system, the state of California might have to borrow $100 billion, which is equal to 75% of all the tax income the state collects in one year.

Imagine if you had to borrow an amount that’s three quarters of your yearly income.

It would be pretty hard to pay back the loan.

California would put itself in a similarly difficult financial situation even if it saved some money on road maintenance.

Second, trains only reduce traffic congestion on the roads if people find taking the train more convenient than driving.

But this largely depends on how convenient it is for people to access the train stations.

In the east coast cities, people can get to the rail stations easily thanks to extensive public transportation systems, but convenient public transportation is often lacking in the urban areas on the west coast.

If Californians cannot reach the stations easily, many will probably keep driving their cars instead of taking the trains and the roads will stay congested.

Third, the environmental benefits.

The problem is that a new high speed track would be built for some of the route, but not for the whole route.

To make the best use of available resources, the California high speed trains would travel on already existing regular tracks for some parts of the route.

But since the regular tracks don’t allow for high speed travel, the high speed trains will have to slow down for parts of the route.

That slowing down will make the new trains much less fuel efficient and fuel emissions will not be reduced as much as the Reading claims.

阅读 The Collapse of Copán

The ancient Mayan kingdom of Copán, in what is now western Honduras, flourished for many years in the first millennium but declined sharply in the eighth or ninth century c.e. A major factor in this collapse was the failure of its ruling dynasty to retain its legitimacy or to solve Copán’s problems. Like their counterparts in ancient Egypt and China, Mayan rulers promoted themselves as guarantors of balance and harmony in the cosmos and of the well-being of their kingdoms. Between the sixth and the ninth centuries, the Mayan world was increasingly perturbed by disorder resulting from many causes, and we have no clear evidence that kings, or for that matter their associated officials and nobility, ever took effective and practical managerial action to contend with developing crises. Instead, kings probably responded with timetested rituals aimed at averting or regulating chaos. No matter how well these seemed to work in earlier times in Copán, they clearly failed at the end. The Copán royal dynasty was blamed for the situation by the lesser elite. Such a situation would explain many things, including the apparent weakness of King Yax Pasa during the last part of his reign in the early ninth century, his abrupt departure, the feeble and unsuccessful attempts to continue his dynastic line, the halt in royal construction and monument carving that took place at this time, and the abandonment of the old royal sections of the city. The dynastic rule was ultimately rejected because of its manifest inability to deliver on the order it promised.

Another explanation for Copán’s collapse is based on the idea that it derived much of its wealth and prestige from is the brokering of commerce that connected the Mayan Lowlands proper with the highlands of southeastern Central America and the interior valleys of central Honduras. Disruption of this commerce might consequently have contributed to this collapse. However, this is a dubious proposition; field research shows that little exotic or foreign material actually shows up in archaeological contexts (as would be expected for a city specializing in trade), and imports from the core of the Mayan Lowlands are particularly sparse. Most of what we do find is marine shell, jade, fancy pottery, minerals such as cinnabar and pyrite, and other items consumed mainly by the elite people. Not only is traffic in these things apparently small, but many of them might have wound up at Copán through mechanisms other than trade, such as the exchange of gifts among prominent people. Their importation was probably intermittent, stimulated by the situational demand for fine materials required for specific events such as royal funerals. Only one imported material-obsidian (volcanic black glass used for jewelry and weaponry)-shows up ubiquitously in excavations at Copán. Calculations show that it was procured on a small annual scale, and clearly it was a sufficiently cheap commodity that everyone had access to it. There seemed to be no drop-off in its availability after kings (and eventually nobles) disappeared from the scene, so its flow was never in fact disrupted.

Other scholars have tried to force Copán’s decline into the theory attributing the collapse of Mayan states to a long and severe drought during this period. But the archaeological facts as we know them do not fit very well We certainly have no evidence that the Copán River or its tributaries ever dried up, depriving the local populations of drinking water. What fits this theory best is the dynastic collapse around 800 c ., just when the drought is supposed to have begun. But even here the coincidence is suspect-dynastic stresses apparently started to build up a generation earlier. More revealing is the disjunction between the demographic profile and the predictions of the drought theory. Populations remained near peak levels for at least the first century of the presumed drought interval, and more than half the people were still there in 950 c.e. Even elite activity flickered on until about the time the drought is supposed to have ended. None of this is consistent with a devastating dry interval.
